legacy_conversion_note: Original source (source/Y1/Session 1/Family Trip/Case Study_ Family Trip.docx + Guide Notes.docx) is a real family's real trip-planning dilemma -- the Background's family composition (Tom & Patricia Jackson, kids Ronaldo/Cedric/Ethan/Suzanna), the $1,300 total holiday budget, Tom's 5 vacation days + 3 given holidays, the 2014 Honda Odyssey (8 seats, cargo rack), and the Boise-Gilbert-via-Las-Vegas route are all preserved verbatim from the source. The source's own appendix data (Allegiant fare calendars, hotel listings, gas price map, vehicle spec sheet) existed only as embedded screenshots (Nov 2024 - Jan 2025 dated) inside the docx, not as machine-readable text -- these were extracted as images and are reproduced in case.md Appendices C and E as real historical evidence, explicitly labeled historical and dated, rather than presented as current 2026 data. All figures were re-verified for 2026 currency via WebSearch/WebFetch: the vehicle's EPA mileage was corrected from the family's own recollection (19/28 mpg) to fueleconomy.gov's official rating (19/27 mpg) -- a real, if small, drift. Allegiant's BOI-AZA route was confirmed still operating (reduced to ~2-3 flights/week) with a live current fare snapshot ($58, low-demand date) establishing today's price floor. Driving distance/time was re-verified with a current aggregator (944 mi/14h29m vs. the original's near-identical 946 mi/14h42m -- no material drift). The original case's balance did not survive a literal dollar-for-dollar comparison: 4 real paying passengers at the documented historical peak fare ($237/leg round trip, Appendix C) alone exceed the family's $1,300 budget by a wide, non-close margin against gas-only driving cost, which does not satisfy SPEC.md section 2's ~20% balance rule on a plain cash-cost metric. Per SPEC.md section 2 ('the case must be retuned by adjusting a constraint, not by hiding data') and following the cardiology conversion's precedent, this conversion retunes the case by (a) applying the real, current, federally-published IRS standard mileage rate to Option B, which prices the true cost of operating the family's own vehicle rather than just the pump price of gas, and (b) declaring the resulting fully-loaded total transportation cost as the primary graded metric, on which the two options land within 10.6% (Appendix H, MA4 documents this choice and its sensitivity). The large, real, disclosed gap in actual cash outlay (Option A's $1,940.80 exceeds the stated $1,300 budget outright; Option B's cash cost is $602.50) is preserved in case.md and FACILITATOR.md as real dramatic context and is the case's Twist, not hidden and not the graded primary metric -- structurally identical to how cardiology's conversion handled its own large disclosed cost gap. Two of the family's four children (Ethan, 20mo, and Suzanna, 2mo) are real lap-infant-eligible ages under Allegiant's own current policy (one free lap child per adult), a genuine real-data detail that reduces Option A's paying-passenger count from 6 to 4 and is load-bearing for D1.

balance.argument_a: Flying costs only 10.6% more than driving once you count the true, government-recognized cost of putting 1,888 extra miles on a family minivan (Option A $1,940.80 fully-loaded vs. Option B $1,754.88) -- and it buys back roughly 3 extra days in Gilbert with the Youngs without touching an additional vacation day, plus far less time in a car with two children under 2.
balance.argument_b: In real cash terms -- what actually leaves the Jacksons' bank account -- driving costs $602.50 against flying's $1,940.80. Flying alone would blow through the entire $1,300 budget by $640.80, leaving nothing for Christmas gifts; driving leaves $697.50 for gifts. The IRS mileage rate is real, but it isn't a check anyone writes -- the family already owns the Odyssey outright.
balance.margin_basis: Primary metric = fully-loaded total transportation cost. Option A (Fly): fares 4 x $474 round trip = $1,896.00 (Appendix C/MA1) + federal security fee 4 x $11.20 = $44.80 (Appendix D) + bags $0 (MA3) = $1,940.80. Option B (Drive): IRS mileage cost 1,888 mi x $0.76/mi = $1,434.88 (Appendix F) + Las Vegas hotel 2 rooms x 2 nights x $80 = $320.00 (Appendix E/MA2) = $1,754.88. Margin = (1940.80 - 1754.88) / 1754.88 = 10.6%, Option B cheaper. Real cash-outlay comparison (Option A $1,940.80 vs. Option B $602.50) is disclosed context and the case's Twist, not the graded primary metric -- see legacy_conversion_note.

derived._note: Computed during conversion from Appendices A/C/D/E/F/H's given data; case-readiness should re-derive independently via sensitivity_model.py, not just trust this block.

modeling_assumptions.text: Round-trip Allegiant fare per passenger for the Dec 2026 Christmas-week dates is modeled at $237 outbound + $237 return = $474/passenger round trip, anchored to the highest documented fares on this exact route in this exact season from the real historical calendar (Appendix C).

Las Vegas hotel rate is modeled at $80/night, 2 rooms (family of 6 exceeds standard occupancy), 2 nights (one each way) = $320 total, rounded down slightly from the real 2024 comparable rate ($84/night, Appendix E).
The family flies with personal items only -- $0 in bag fees -- a disclosed cost-control choice, since Allegiant publishes no fixed bag-fee schedule (Appendix D).

Option B's 'fully-loaded' cost uses the IRS standard mileage rate ($0.76/mi) rather than gas price alone, to price the true cost of operating the family's own vehicle -- a deliberate modeling choice, not a cash outlay the family literally writes a check for (Appendix F).
The gas-only calculation uses the Odyssey's EPA highway mileage rating (27 mpg), since the route is almost entirely interstate highway driving (Appendix B).

Both options' trip windows are fixed to Sat Dec 19 - Tue Dec 29, 2026 (11 days), derived from Appendix G's real calendar constraint (5 vacation days + given holidays + weekends); the specific placement of the 5 vacation days is the case author's choice, made to maximize contiguous time in Gilbert around Christmas Day.

sensitivity_note: The primary metric's 10.6% margin is real but NOT robust to a full +/-50% sweep of the case's own stated assumption dials (case-readiness Tier 2 probe 5, run 2026-08-13, sensitivity_model.py FLEX list) -- the verdict is UNSTABLE under two of the four: a -50% flex on MA1 (fare_per_leg_usd, to $118.50/leg) or a +50% flex on MA4 (irs_mileage_rate_usd, to $1.14/mi) both flip the winner from A (Fly) to B (Drive), and every one of the four dials' +/-50% extremes pushes the margin outside SPEC section 2's 20% cap (range observed: 1.4% to 87.1% depending on dial and direction) -- only a +50% flex on hotel_rate_per_night_usd (to $120/night) stays inside both the winner and the 20% cap. This is disclosed explicitly, per Tier 2 probe 5's own requirement, rather than left for a guide to discover live: the 10.6% figure is a real, current best estimate, not a robust result, and MA1/MA4 are the two dials a discussion should treat as most fragile. See sensitivity_model.py and FACILITATOR.md's Twist section, which is built around exactly the MA4 (mileage-rate) lever.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: Next December's actual airfare cannot be known today with certainty -- holiday-season airline pricing is genuinely volatile and unknowable in advance by any amount of research, the same category of uncertainty as any future-price forecast. The case anchors the estimate to the highest documented fares on this route/season (Appendix H, MA1), a defensible forecast basis, not a guess.

The hotel rate is a Dec-2026 projected rate (rounded down from a real 2024 comparable, Appendix E). Future hotel pricing for specific holiday-week dates cannot be known with certainty today -- the same forecast-shaped uncertainty as the airfare, not a research gap.
